citation: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: A predictable set of educator teams — freshman success, instructional leadership, postsecondary leadership, senior leadership, and care — drives improvement in NCS partner high schools
description: The paper describes the teaming structures used to drive improvement in NCS partner high schools, where visiting educators would likely find a predictable set of teams. Table A lays out five common teams with their members, responsibilities, and data: a Freshman Success Team monitoring the transition into high school using GPA, grades, attendance, behavior, and eighth-grade early warning data; an Instructional Leadership Team working on instructional coherence; a Postsecondary Leadership Team supporting college search, application, and enrollment; a Senior Leadership Team setting vision and monitoring high-level data; and a Care Team of specialists intervening with socially vulnerable students. A common collaboration rhythm is a bi-weekly meeting of roughly 45-60 minutes in which teams analyze data, set intervention strategies, and progress monitor. The paper argues distributed leadership and teaming structures are crucial for driving teacher collaboration at scale in large, complex high schools.
requirements: Distributed leadership and teaming structures, with administrator support for each team
Dedicated meeting time in which teams analyze student data and monitor interventions
constraints: Team structures look different across schools, and the paper notes high schools are often large, complex organizations where individual educators have limited time to collaborate
target_learners: high school teacher teams and administrators
target_learning_goals: monitoring student transitions and academic achievement
organizing school-wide improvement efforts around shared data
examples: Table A specifies, for instance, that the Freshman Success Team uses GPA, course grades, attendance rates, behavioral data, and eighth-grade early warning indicator data to monitor students' transition into high school
key_sources: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/practice-driven-data-lessons-chicagos-approach-research-data-and-practice-education

citation: Pitcher, M. A., Duncan, S. J., Nagaoka, J., Moeller, E., Dickerson, L., & Beechum, N. O. (2016). The Network for College Success: A Capacity-Building Model for School Improvement. University of Chicago. https://ncs.uchicago.edu
title: The NCS capacity-building model for school improvement
description: The Network for College Success model is a whole-school improvement framework that builds the systems, structures, and capacity of school staff rather than adopting an external reform package. It is organized around four key elements: "1. Creating Professional Learning Networks; 2. Applying Research-Based Data to Practice; 3. Coaching and Capacity Building; and 4. Distributing Leadership and Building High-Functioning Teams." NCS embeds learning in sustained professional learning communities working toward long-term goals, provides job-embedded coaching to school leaders, and positions principals as primary drivers of change who must distribute leadership across staff. The paper illustrates the model through the Freshman On Track work in Chicago Public Schools.
requirements: Sustained, long-term partnerships rather than one-time professional development, because the paper states one-time drive-by professional development is insufficient for deep and lasting change
constraints: The paper states it is not an evaluation of NCS nor evidence of its efficacy; it documents the model and stakeholder experiences
target_learners: High school principals, teacher leaders, counselors, and data strategists in urban districts
target_learning_goals: School leaders' capacity to use research-based data, lead collaborative improvement, and raise freshman success and graduation rates
examples: NCS facilitated cross-school Collaboratives for principals, counselors, teacher leaders, and data strategists, and provided job-embedded coaching to school leaders in 32 partner schools over 10 years
key_sources: Pitcher, M. A., Duncan, S. J., Nagaoka, J., Moeller, E., Dickerson, L., & Beechum, N. O. (2016). The Network for College Success: A Capacity-Building Model for School Improvement. University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/network-college-success-capacity-building-model-school-improvement

article_title: STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: From Good Teachers to Great Teaching
citation: Kathleen Fulton & Ted Britton. (2011). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: From Good Teachers to Great Teaching. National Commission on Teaching and America's Future. http://www.nctaf.org/documents/STEMTeachersinProfessionalLearningCommunities.AKnowledgeSynthesis.pdf
title: NCTAF STEM learning studios with cross-curricular teams and STEM professional volunteers
description: NCTAF's STEM learning teams work in "STEM learning studios": intentionally cross-curricular teams of science, math, and technology teachers joined by scientists and engineers from government, business, and industry who co-design and implement project-based learning activities addressing learning challenges the teachers identify. Implementation begins with a three-day summer workshop and quarterly design sessions, typically teaching one inquiry-based project module per quarter. Launched in 2009 with a NASA grant, the model reached eight high schools in three Maryland districts as of Spring 2011.
requirements: STEM industry and government volunteers recruited based on expertise matching the teachers' identified learning challenges
constraints: The report describes the model's first-year evaluation only; it does not present controlled achievement evidence for the studios
target_learners: High school and middle school teachers and students in participating Maryland districts
target_learning_goals: Enhancing STEM teaching through cross-disciplinary project-based learning
examples: An independent first-year evaluation showed an almost immediate positive impact on both teachers and students
Approximately three-quarters of students said what they learned in class helped them better understand the world around them
key_sources: Kathleen Fulton & Ted Britton. (2011). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: From Good Teachers to Great Teaching. National Commission on Teaching and America's Future. http://www.nctaf.org/documents/STEMTeachersinProfessionalLearningCommunities.AKnowledgeSynthesis.pdf

article_title: Evaluation of the Comprehensive School Reform Program Implementation and Outcomes. Fifth-Year Report
citation: Orland, M., Hoffman, A., & Vaughn, III, E. S. (2010). Evaluation of the Comprehensive School Reform Program Implementation and Outcomes: Fifth-Year Report. U.S. Department of Education. https://www.ed.gov/about/offices/list/opepd/ppss/reports.html#title
title: NCLB eleven-component comprehensive school reform framework
description: The NCLB legislation defines comprehensive school reform as a coordinated approach requiring that "school reform should be comprehensive in nature, strengthening all aspects of school operations—curriculum, instruction, professional development, parental involvement and school organization." The framework specifies 11 components assumed to work together, including proven methods based on scientific research, comprehensive design, professional development, measurable goals, staff support, parent and community involvement, external assistance, evaluation, coordination of resources, and use of scientifically based research models with evidence of effectiveness in multiple settings.
requirements: Schools must implement all 11 components together for reform to be comprehensive as legislatively defined
constraints: The framework was legislatively specified under NCLB Title I, Part F, Section 1606
target_learners: K-12 public school students in low-performing Title I schools
target_learning_goals: Meeting state performance standards in mathematics and reading
examples: The ECSRIO study surveyed 436 CSR and 382 non-CSR schools to measure implementation of these 11 components
key_sources: Orland, M., Hoffman, A., & Vaughn, III, E. S. (2010). Evaluation of the Comprehensive School Reform Program Implementation and Outcomes: Fifth-Year Report. U.S. Department of Education. https://www.ed.gov/about/offices/list/opepd/ppss/reports.html#title

article_title: Knowledge without Wisdom: Measuring Misalignment between LLMs and Intended Impact
citation: Michael Hardy, Yunsung Kim. (2026). Knowledge without Wisdom: Measuring Misalignment between LLMs and Intended Impact. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00883
title: NCTE Main Study dataset of classroom observations with expert ratings and value-added measures
description: The National Center for Teacher Effectiveness (NCTE) Main Study dataset provides the study's core data. The article states it "comprises ob- servations of roughly 350 4th and 5th-grade math- ematics teachers across four U.S. school districts." It is described as one of only two educational datasets containing measures of teaching practice, authentic classroom artifacts, and student learning outcomes at scale (VAMs). The study used anonymized transcripts of video-recorded lessons from its test set, rated by 63 MQI raters and 19 CLASS raters with rigorous certification and continual calibration.
requirements: requires linking of expert observation ratings with value-added measures of student learning, a combination the article says exists in only two extant datasets
constraints: the transcript data contain only fourth- and fifth-grade mathematics classrooms from the United States, limiting generalization to all classrooms
target_learners: 4th and 5th grade mathematics students in four U.S. school districts
target_learning_goals: student mathematics achievement growth measured by value-added scores
examples: The study prompted 16 LLMs on 479 lesson transcripts from 311 classrooms drawn from this dataset's test set, evaluating alignment against MQI and CLASS expert ratings and stacked VAMs
key_sources: Michael Hardy, Yunsung Kim. (2026). Knowledge without Wisdom: Measuring Misalignment between LLMs and Intended Impact. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00883

article_title: A Half Century of Progress in US Student Achievement: Agency and Flynn Effects, Ethnic and SES Differences
citation: M. Danish Shakeel · Paul E. Peterson. (2022). A Half Century of Progress in US Student Achievement: Agency and Flynn Effects, Ethnic and SES Differences. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09657-y
title: NCES restricted-use individual-level dataset of seven million US student observations across 160 survey waves
description: The study's empirical base is individual-student data from the NCES restricted-use dataset, covering "Approximately seven million student-level observations of US students and approximately four and a half million observations of non-US students". The data span 160 waves of 17 psychometrically linked surveys in math and reading administered to national probability samples of cohorts born between 1954 and 2007, with survey weights applied and the second plausible value used per wave.
requirements: Access restricted to qualified research centers; parental education and possession-index measures are unavailable in some survey waves
constraints: Ethnicity information is missing for PIRLS 2001 and 2016; NAEP 12th-grade math trends are included only for students born after 1987 because earlier tests were not psychometrically linked
target_learners: US students aged 9, 13, 15, and 17 and in grades 4, 8, and 12
target_learning_goals: Measuring change over time in math and reading achievement
examples: The SES index is extracted as the first principal component of the household possession index and parental education categories, available for 15 surveys.
key_sources: M. Danish Shakeel · Paul E. Peterson. (2022). A Half Century of Progress in US Student Achievement: Agency and Flynn Effects, Ethnic and SES Differences. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09657-y

article_title: Educational strategies and nursing theory to prepare leaners for NCLEX-RN.
citation: Almasloukh, K. B., Miner, M., Phillips, K., & Evans, M. (2023). Educational strategies and nursing theory to prepare leaners for NCLEX‐RN. Nursing Open, 10, 7144–7153. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.1998
title: Eight theories/models recur across NCLEX-RN preparation literature, with Tanner's clinical judgement model aligned stepwise to the NCSBN Clinical Judgement Measurement Model
description: The review identifies eight theories or models used in more than one reviewed article: Tanner's clinical judgement model, the NCJMM, Knowles' adult learning theory (andragogy), Bloom's three learning domains, Peplau's theory of interpersonal relations, Bandura's self-efficacy theory, self-determination theory of motivation, and Astin's input-environment-outcome model. The review maps Tanner's steps onto the NCJMM: "The first step in Tanner's clinical judgement model is noticing," paralleled by recognizing and analysing cues, through to reflection paralleled by refining hypotheses and evaluation. Theories were used in 19 of the reviewed studies.
requirements: Theories are used as frameworks guiding educational strategies for NCLEX-RN preparation, as charted across the 25 reviewed studies
constraints: The review found no favoured theory or framework that should guide NCLEX-RN preparation, and no clearly defined theory focusing on students' QOL
target_learners: pre-licensure nursing students preparing for the NCLEX-RN
target_learning_goals: clinical judgement
NCLEX-RN readiness
critical thinking
examples: The review's Table 3 lists the eight theories with their citing articles; the discussion details stepwise similarities between Tanner's model and the NCJMM
key_sources: Almasloukh, K. B., Miner, M., Phillips, K., & Evans, M. (2023). Educational strategies and nursing theory to prepare leaners for NCLEX‐RN. Nursing Open, 10, 7144–7153. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.1998

article_title: The Effect of Brain Based Learning on Second Grade Junior Students' Mathematics Conceptual Understanding on Polyhedron
citation: Suarsana, I.M., Widiasih, N.P.S., & Suparta, I.N. (2018). The effect of brain based learning on second grade junior students’ mathematics conceptual understanding on polyhedron. Journal on Mathematics Education, 9(1), 145-156. https://jme.ejournal.unsri.ac.id
title: Essay post-test of mathematical conceptual understanding based on NCTM indicators
description: The study's instrument was an essay test designed according to NCTM (2000) conceptual-understanding indicators: "describe concepts in their own words", "identify or give examples and non-examples of concepts", and "use correctly concepts in a variety of situations". Content validity was checked by Gregory testing (trustworthy at 0,70 or above per Gay, 1996), item validity by Pearson product-moment correlation, and reliability by Alpha Cronbach with a criterion of r11 > 0,40.
requirements: Instrument must pass content validity, item validity, and reliability checks as described
constraints: Used only as a post-test in the polyhedron quasi-experiment
target_learners: grade VIII junior high school students
target_learning_goals: mathematical conceptual understanding
examples: The abstract describes the post-test as containing 8 essay question types on mathematical conceptual understanding
key_sources: Suarsana, I.M., Widiasih, N.P.S., & Suparta, I.N. (2018). The effect of brain based learning on second grade junior students’ mathematics conceptual understanding on polyhedron. Journal on Mathematics Education, 9(1), 145-156. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1173645

article_title: Evaluating the Impact of NCLB School Interventions in New York State: Does One Size Fit All?
citation: Lee, J., Shin, H. & Amo, L. C. (2013). Evaluating the impact of NCLB school interventions in New York state: Does one size fit all? Education Policy Analysis Archives, 21 (67). http://epaa.asu.edu/ojs/article/view/1122
title: NCLB test-driven accountability theory of action: sanctions and mandated interventions pressure lagging schools to make larger gains toward proficiency
description: The article describes the working theory of test-driven school accountability policy: "such policy can bring about significant change in educational practice and academic improvement by holding schools accountable for test results with possible sanctions and interventions." Under NCLB, schools failing AYP for two consecutive years move through sequential intervention stages — school transfer, SES, corrective action, planning for restructuring, and restructuring — with the quantity and intensity of supports and monitoring increasing over time. The study's matched findings of negative or null effects challenge this theory of action at the school level.
requirements: Schools must respond to the threat of sanctions and interventions by improving practice, per the theory's assumption that "schools want to avoid potential stigma attached to public identifications"
constraints: The study's matched results found the theory's predicted larger gains for treated schools did not materialize, and the article questions whether a "one size fits all" approach to mandated interventions can work at the school level
target_learners: Students in New York State public schools identified for improvement under NCLB
target_learning_goals: Reading/ELA and mathematics proficiency as measured by state assessments
examples: New York State's Regional Network Strategy provided technical assistance through Regional School Support Centers and related centers for schools and districts required to improve
key_sources: Lee, J., Shin, H. & Amo, L. C. (2013). Evaluating the impact of NCLB school interventions in New York state: Does one size fit all? Education Policy Analysis Archives, 21 (67). http://epaa.asu.edu/ojs/article/view/1122

article_title: Development of vignette-based evaluation with generative artificial intelligence (VEGA) for nursing students: a pilot study.
citation: Shin Sujin, Choi Jaehwa, Hong Eunmin, Lee Miji, Go Jinseon, Yu Subin, Lee Minjae. (2026). Development of vignette-based evaluation with generative artificial intelligence (VEGA) for nursing students: a pilot study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09685-8
title: NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model (NCJMM) as the structural framework for AI-generated vignette items
description: The NCJMM, developed by NCSBN, "delineates a six-step clinical judgment process: recognizing cues, analyzing cues, prioritizing hypotheses, generating solutions, taking action, and evaluating outcomes." In VEGA, each of the six stages shaped item structure, with one item per stage and prompt instructions operationalized to reflect each step's cognitive demands. This alignment ensured item sets were clinically contextualized and pedagogically grounded in a recognized nursing framework.
requirements: Prompt instructions must explicitly operationalize the cognitive demands of each of the six stages to prevent overlap between stages
target_learners: nursing students preparing for the Next Generation NCLEX
target_learning_goals: clinical judgment: recognizing cues, analyzing cues, prioritizing hypotheses, generating solutions, taking action, evaluating outcomes
examples: Each vignette generated by VEGA was paired with six NCJMM-aligned items, one per stage
key_sources: Shin Sujin, Choi Jaehwa, Hong Eunmin, Lee Miji, Go Jinseon, Yu Subin, Lee Minjae. (2026). Development of vignette-based evaluation with generative artificial intelligence (VEGA) for nursing students: a pilot study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09685-8

article_title: The Role of the Simulation in Supporting Newly Graduated Nurses in Their First 5 Months of Working Transition: Findings From a Mixed-Method Study.
citation: Mesaglio, M., Dentice, S., Grassetti, L., Achil, I., Bernardinis, A., Caruzzo, D., Inserra, A., Mansutti, I., Mattiussi, E., Menegoz, S., Piani, T., Vanzo, E., Chiappinotto, S., Palese, A. (2026). The Role of the Simulation in Supporting Newly Graduated Nurses in Their First 5 Months of Working Transition: Findings From a Mixed‐Method Study. Journal of Clinical Nursing, 35(10), 4210–4220. https://doi.org/10.1111/jocn.17617
title: Nurse Competence Scale (NCS) as a longitudinal self-assessment tool for newly graduated nurses' transition
description: The Nurse Competence Scale is a validated instrument with "73 items divided into seven dimensions": helping role, teaching–coaching, diagnostic functions, managing situations, therapeutic interventions, quality assurance, and working role. It measures perceived competence on a visual analogue scale from 0 to 100, with scores below 60 indicating insufficient competence. In this study it was administered at four time points over 5 months with high internal consistency (Cronbach's α 0.983–0.992).
requirements: Respondents must self-assess on a VAS from 0 to 100; the study used an online platform (EUSurvey) for data collection
constraints: Self-assessment may result in under- or overestimation of competencies; the study's cut-off of below 60 for insufficient competence may be restrictive compared to the literature
target_learning_goals: self-assessment of professional competencies across seven domains
examples: Used longitudinally at T0 (first day of work), T1 (15 days), T2 (3 months) and T3 (5 months) with 151 NGRNs

article_title: Feasibility Evaluation of a Standalone Virtual Reality System for Neonatal Resuscitation Training.
citation: Amari Shoichiro, Eto Masato, Oyama Hiroshi. (2026). Feasibility Evaluation of a Standalone Virtual Reality System for Neonatal Resuscitation Training. Journal of Medical Systems 50:94. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10916-026-02423-z
title: NCPR-VR: standalone, instructor-free VR application for neonatal resuscitation skill maintenance
description: NCPR-VR is a Unity-developed application on a Meta Quest 3 standalone head-mounted display that "was designed to operate entirely offline." It comprises three sequential scenes—pre-training, training, and post-training—delivering scenario presentation and structured feedback "without involvement of NCPR instructors," focused on initiating positive-pressure ventilation within 60 s of birth under the Japanese NCPR 2020 guideline.
requirements: Requires a commercially available standalone head-mounted display with handheld controllers; no internet connection or additional equipment
constraints: Not intended as a standalone procedural training tool for pre-certification novices, nor a replacement for initial certification or mannequin-based SBT; bag–mask haptics not faithfully reproduced
target_learners: already-certified perinatal healthcare professionals (physicians, nurses, midwives) with limited access to on-the-job resuscitation or off-the-job simulation
target_learning_goals: maintaining neonatal resuscitation skills, particularly initiating and sustaining effective positive-pressure ventilation within the first 60 s after birth
examples: In the study, 32 certified providers progressed through the pre-training, training, and post-training scenes with a 100% completion rate
key_sources: Amari Shoichiro, Eto Masato, Oyama Hiroshi. (2026). Feasibility Evaluation of a Standalone Virtual Reality System for Neonatal Resuscitation Training. Journal of Medical Systems 50:94. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10916-026-02423-z

article_title: Inequities in the National Clinical Assessment Tool for Medical Students in the Emergency Department.
citation: Amin Bushra Z., Dine C. J., Tabakin E. R., Trotter M., Heath J. K. (2025). Inequities in the National Clinical Assessment Tool for Medical Students in the Emergency Department. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.43506
title: NCAT-EM: National Clinical Assessment Tool for Emergency Medicine
description: The NCAT-EM is a nationally standardized, specialty-specific assessment tool developed in 2016 via consensus to standardize medical student assessment during emergency medicine rotations. It consists of "six clinical performance domains rated on a four-point entrustability scale, a global assessment domain, a professionalism section, and mandatory free-text comments". It has begun replacing institution-specific tools across US EM rotations and informs clerkship grades, the MSPE, and SLOEs.
requirements: Completed at every shift via a QR code linking to an online platform, presented by students to attending or supervising resident raters
constraints: Prior work noted site-specific variation in ratings, suggesting limitations in the response process of validity or generalizability of the tool
target_learners: medical students on emergency medicine clerkships
target_learning_goals: clinical performance domains including history/physical, differential diagnosis, plan formulation, observation/monitoring, emergency management, and communication
examples: Used at the University of Pennsylvania since 2018; 1,881 forms were analyzed in this study
key_sources: Amin Bushra Z., Dine C. J., Tabakin E. R., Trotter M., Heath J. K. (2025). Inequities in the National Clinical Assessment Tool for Medical Students in the Emergency Department. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.43506

article_title: The relationship between caring ability and communication competence among nursing staff in Chinese tertiary hospitals: A cross-sectional and analytical study.
citation: Jing, C., Feng, D., Zheng, D., Hu, L., Yuan, F., Xiao, Y., Zhu, S., & Liu, X. (2025). The relationship between caring ability and communication competence among nursing staff in Chinese tertiary hospitals: A cross-sectional and analytical study. Scientific Reports, 15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-19896-6
title: Nurses' Clinic Communication Competency Scale (NCCCS) and Caring Ability Inventory (CAI) as paired self-report measures
description: The study operationalizes two self-report instruments administered online: the NCCCS, which "included six dimensions" covering team, basic language, basic non-language, emotional perception, emotional support, and difficult-clinical-scenes competency (58 items, Likert 5-point, range 58–290), and the Chinese CAI (37 items, Likert 7-point) with knowing, courage, and patience dimensions. In this sample Cronbach's alpha was 0.995 for NCCCS and 0.856 for CAI. The pair enables correlated assessment of caring and communication competence in practicing nurses.
requirements: Respondents hold a nurse qualification and work in direct patient contact, per the study's inclusion criteria
constraints: Self-report measures, which the article notes may introduce bias
target_learning_goals: clinical communication competency
caring ability
examples: Administered via the wenjuanxing online platform to 3,000 invited nurses, yielding 2,050 responses and 1,977 valid questionnaires after validity screening.

article_title: Sharp increase in inequality in education in times of the COVID-19-pandemic.
citation: Haelermans Carla, Korthals Roxanne, Jacobs Madelon, de Leeuw Suzanne, Vermeulen Stan, van Vugt Lynn, Aarts Bas, Prokic-Breuer Tijana, van der Velden Rolf, van Wetten Sanne, de Wolf Inge. (2022). Sharp increase in inequality in education in times of the COVID-19-pandemic. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0261114
title: NCO standardized test score dataset with midterm-to-end-of-term learning gains for Dutch primary students
description: The element is the linked dataset of standardized test scores (CITO and other suppliers) and register background data from the Netherlands Cohort Study on Education, covering school years 2013/2014 to 2019/2020 with 1,319 schools and 291,635 unique students gathered, 201,819 students in 1,178 schools after cleaning. "The learning gains are defined based on the standardized test scores and are calculated by subtracting the score on the midterm test from the end-of-term test of each domain within a school year". Top and bottom 1% of absolute learning gains are excluded to remove outliers.
requirements: Students must have taken a midterm and end-of-term test within the same school year at the same school
constraints: Data cannot be shared publicly because they are part of the data at Statistics Netherlands and cannot be exported from the secured virtual environment
target_learners: Primary school students in grades 1 to 6 in the Netherlands
target_learning_goals: Reading
Spelling
Mathematics
examples: Test records per domain: reading 201,819, spelling 269,774, math 311,439 (Table 2)
